title: How are we dealing with model output licensing?
author: Seven-Prime
selftext:
tl,dr; Do we care? 


As I'm ramping up my asset generation pipeline with ComfyUI and a mix of local and hosted models, some licensing questions come up from Claude. For example Tencent carries an EU-withholding flag.


Personal development at the moment, but hope to ship at some point. Evil me says they didn't bother licensing, so why should I? On the other hand, they have lawyers on retainer.


What are our thoughts?

comments.author: Vivid-Snow-2089
comments.body:
imagine the model maker put a hidden watermark in it, you ignore their license, you make a ton of money, and  they find out you violated their license, and now your tons of money suddenly has to defend itself in a lawsuit

depends on lots of factors like where are you at and how likely are you to be sued in your country's courts, how likely you are to do well or make enough to be a target, if they want to just make example of easy to reach targets who violate the license, yadda yadda... i mean just think about it a bit or ask your LLM to help you consider the problems with ignoring a license

although my advice is don't do stupid shit like purposefully violate licenses because you think you'll get away with it, because that type of behavior always fucks the person up in the end

replies.author: Seven-Prime
replies.body: thanks for responding m8. Defo trying to do the right thing. Gathering this license info is one of those 'hidden' activities of game development than can trap newbs like me. At least with my enterprise dev experience it is on my radar. I'd hate to deal with this later.

comments.author: w1a1s1p
comments.body:
Been in the same boat with you, and the conclusion is everyone is a cowboy until they aren't. 
A lawsuit is not likely, but takedown is fast and easy, imagine getting your product taken down because of license, that would be a real blow.

That's why I redid many assets with tools that don't have licensing issues.
You can also reach out to the tool or service provider and ask for a license (haven't done that myself, but this was the overall suggestion)

replies.author: Seven-Prime
replies.body:
Good advice. I'm at early stages of having to build a lot of assets. I did my flora with bespoke claude and blender with available plugins.

But now I have a growing list of assets to create and need to be more careful.

comments.author: Mindestiny
comments.body:
Track the provenance of everything you're using, right down to date and model version.  Just keep it in a google doc or something.

Then you can navigate the risk coherently with whatever assets survive to release state.  But definitely make sure you're obeying all licensing and not just YOLOing it hoping no one will notice.  Especially with more recent watermarking efforts, expect this to be a legitimate legal issue in a few years and not just something no one cares about.  OpenAI is going to want a slice of your pie when their AI agents are skimming Steam and your game gets flagged as using assets with their watermarking, etc.

replies.author: Seven-Prime
replies.body:
Thanks m8. I'll ensure I'm tracking the provenance of my asset generation. It'll go into my art cannon repo where I'm organizing all these things. I'm already tracking plate and reference image licenses.

The assets I'm creating aren't one shots to image assets. Quite a bit of iteration on them. But your point still stands. At least the big players will pay for my game to skim it right? They won't violate my TOS and decompile the code right? RIGHT?

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body: Yeah, that's the catch.  You could ChatGPT some concept image or whatever then pull it into photoshop and edit 90% of it, but that last 10% could still be hiding coherent watermarks where they could identify it as their own generated content.  Nobody wants to wind up in a legal battle fighting over "how much editing makes it derivative and thus no longer under the terms of the license."

replies.author: darkoblivion000
replies.body: Hold on… are we saying that openAI automatically owns the rights to every image they produce? Or that that legal battle hasn’t been decided yet but into the future they could potentially retroactively own the rights and then come after anyone who used their image generation? Or blender mesh generated?

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
The answer is "we don't know." Even if they don't blanket own all rights to the content in perpetuity, there's almost certainly a licensing structure where *you* need a license grant from them to use their content commercially.  Today that could be included with a paid plan, tomorrow it could be restricted to some sort of Enterprise/Partner agreement with a separate fee structure associated with it.

The Blender question, and MCP servers in general, are exactly where my head was at too - its one thing to go "hey chatgpt, generate a cat picture" and then you raw dog that on your e-commerce website to sell product.  But what about when you go "hey chatgpt, use this MCP server to guide Blender into authoring a 3D model of a house"?  Can they claim rights to that output?  Are they hiding watermarks in the Blender files?

Only time will tell where the legal framework lands.  Right now it's the wild West and you bet your ass they're going to push a "we have rights to how you use our tech to make money" as far as the courts will let them.

replies.author: kindjie
replies.body:
This. I try to avoid using AI art/sound outside of placeholders for this reason and record where every asset I use from asset packs came from so I have an audit trail in case something slips through.

If you’re working on a commercial game I wouldn’t risk breaking licenses for models or assets. Not worth it.
